About the painting

A vast landscape, within reach.

Explore the complete digital image of Wang Ximeng’s A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains from right to left. The image retains the mounting, inscriptions and seals. The landscape itself has not been repainted.

The moving boat, local water routes, optional sound and twelve stops are an artistic interpretation, not a historical reconstruction. The boat sprite was derived with AI assistance from a painted boat. Sound is off by default; discoveries stay in this browser. Disconnected waterways use fade transitions. The watermill diagram and synthesized water sound are interpretive additions.

Image: the public-domain-marked version on Wikimedia Commons, 39,974 × 1,600 pixels. The original painting is held by the Palace Museum, Beijing.

Image source and usage information ↗

The opening inscription was added by the Qing emperor Qianlong. The Chinese text follows thePalace Museum transcription, centuries after the Northern Song painting. The end of the scroll retains the Yuan-period colophon by Puguang.

操作：On mobile, swipe left to advance and right to return. On desktop,向下滚动展开画卷，向上滚动回看。景点自动Zoom in并展开批注；继续滚动退出景点。Explore detail中，滚轮缩放、鼠标左键按住拖动平移，手机双指缩放。点击Continue返回原行程。方向键、空格与全卷导航也可控制行程。

Opening inscription · Qianlong, Qing dynasty

Rivers and mountains without end

An English reading note

The later inscription praises the vast landscape and its spirited brushwork, considers its place in painting traditions, and turns to questions of artistic patronage and rulership.

Read the original Chinese inscription

江山千里望无垠，元气淋漓运以神。
北宋院诚鲜二本，三唐法总弗多皴。
可惊当世王和赵，已讶一堂君若臣。
曷不自思作人者，尔时调鼎作何人。

This is a later Qianlong inscription, not part of the original Northern Song commission.
